key_insight: Audio–language models rarely benefit from clinical multimodal context when transcribing dysarthric speech; adding diagnosis labels or clinician ratings did not reliably reduce recognition errors.
problem_solved: Evaluates whether conditioning ASR on clinical/contextual metadata can help with recognition of dysarthric and atypical speech, exposing a gap between multimodal modeling potential and practical gains on accessibility-focused speech data.
method: Construct a benchmark from the Speech Accessibility Project (SAP) that pairs dysarthric speech with diagnosis labels, clinician-derived speech ratings, and progressively richer clinical context.
Evaluate representative audio–language models by comparing ASR performance with and without each type/level of contextual conditioning; include controlled ablations to isolate effects.
Analyze failure modes and quantify when/why contextual signals fail to improve word/error-level metrics, guiding recommendations for model and dataset design.
impact: Alerts ML practitioners that naive multimodal conditioning may not improve ASR for atypical speech and motivates developing better integration strategies, targeted training data, and evaluation protocols for accessible speech technologies.
visual_elements: Bar chart comparing ASR error rates (e.g., WER): no context vs. diagnosis vs. clinician ratings vs. full clinical context
Schematic diagram of audio–language model showing where contextual metadata is injected (and common failure points)
Dataset flow graphic: SAP recordings → metadata types → benchmark splits/conditions
Example failure case panel: waveform + model transcription with and without context, highlighting unchanged/misrecognized words
paper_title: When Audio-Language Models Fail to Leverage Multimodal Context for Dysarthric Speech Recognition
paper_authors: Pehuén Moure, Niclas Pokel, Bilal Bounajma, Yingqiang Gao, Roman Boehringer
